The situation

Every reading in range, and money leaking between them

See the detail

Your plant treats about 60 million gallons a day, with summer storms. Flow comes in through four variable-speed pumps, then screens and grit removal, then four primary clarifiers. Four aeration basins follow. They use fine-bubble diffusers to feed the biology, remove ammonia, and include a zone without oxygen at the front.

All four basins draw air from one shared header fed by four blowers. Six secondary clarifiers settle the biology, and pumps return or waste the sludge. Ferric chloride is dosed to take out phosphorus. Ultraviolet light then disinfects the water in three channels.

Sludge goes to three digesters. They fill a gas holder and feed a flare and two gas generators that make power and heat for the site. Two centrifuges dewater the digested sludge, and trucks haul the cake away. Odor control and plant water support the whole site.

Most large plants are in this position. The control system keeps each reading inside its limits, and each unit is individually reasonable. What it does not do is notice that one basin, one engine or one centrifuge has quietly stopped behaving like its twins, or that a dose raised for one bad day was never brought back. That is where these losses sit, and why none of them raised an alarm.

The approach

Find the loss, find the cause, price it, confirm it

See the detail

AquaMesh does not assume a fixed percentage. It starts from the plant's existing control-system and historian data and works through five steps.

01Detect

252 measuring points were read from the plant's own records. Every unit was compared with its identical twin, day by day, across 150 days, and every flow and power figure was held up against a balance.

02Diagnose

Each symptom was tested against what the instrument measures and how it typically misleads, to separate process problems from instrument problems. They resolved into 7 causes and 1 reading that needs a field check.

03Price

Each cause was priced from measured quantities, the plant's own curves and its own unit costs, against its own best comparable unit, never a design figure.

04Route a response

Each cause became one specific action with an owner and a timing. AquaMesh recommends; operators decide. Nothing is actuated.

05Verify

Each cause carries a metric and a target, tracked against a baseline from this same record, normalised for load and weather.

CAUSE 1

Ferric chloride is dosed well past the result it is there to buy

$984,221/yrmeasured

Ferric chloride is dosed to take phosphorus out of the water so the effluent meets its permit. The plant's own records give its dose-response: over 150 days the effluent phosphorus follows the ratio of iron dosed to phosphorus load along one curve (R² 0.77). At today's ratio of 1.22 it reaches 0.29 mg/L, against a permit limit of 1.0 mg/L. The curve says a ratio of 0.87 would hold 0.50 mg/L, still half the permit limit. The last part of the dose is the most expensive, because each extra kilogram removes less than the one before. The dose setting went from 10.5 to 12.8 on 18 May and was never brought back.

What the data shows

iron : phosphorus load, molar
Plant's own curve
R² 0.77

Ferric chloride today

What it means

Your own records show the extra iron buys very little additional phosphorus removal, and the effluent is already well under the limit. The dose went up on one day and was never revisited. Left alone, you keep paying for chemical beyond what the result needs. Step it down gradually and watch the effluent phosphorus.

What the operator does

Step the iron dose ratio down toward 0.87 in two or three steps a week apart, holding each until the effluent phosphorus settles, and stop at 0.50 mg/L.

How it is confirmed

Effluent phosphorus and ferric chloride per day. Target: about 0.50 mg/L at about 257 kg/h.

CAUSE 2

Centrifuge 2 leaves more water in its cake than its twin

$568,233/yrmeasured

Centrifuge 2 and centrifuge 1 dewater the same digested sludge. Centrifuge 1 makes cake at 24.4% solids; centrifuge 2 has slid from 23.7% to 20.3%, while using 3.5 kg more polymer per dry tonne. Cake is hauled by the wet tonne, so the water left in it is paid for twice: once in polymer, once in trucks.

What it means

The two centrifuges get the same sludge, so the difference points to the machine or its settings, not the feed. The data fits worn internal parts or a drifted setting, but it cannot tell them apart. Left alone, the cake gets wetter, polymer use grows, and you haul more water.

What the operator does

Inspect centrifuge 2's scroll and wear tiles at the next service window, and reset its differential speed and polymer to centrifuge 1's once it is repaired.

How it is confirmed

Centrifuge 2 cake solids and polymer per dry tonne. Target: 24.4% solids, about 9.1 kg/dry t.

CAUSE 3

Biogas is flared while gas engine 2 runs with room to burn it

$253,762/yrmeasured

The digesters make 864 m³/h of gas. Gas engine 2 burns 267 m³/h of it, 55% of what the engine beside it burns at full load, because its load limit is set at 55%. The gas holder sits full and the flare burns 111 m³/h, gas the engine could have turned into 276 kW the plant now buys from the grid.

CAUSE 4

Disinfection runs at full power on a water-clarity reading that has stopped moving

$161,410/yrmeasured

The ultraviolet system sets its lamp power from the water's ultraviolet transmittance, how much light gets through. Its online reading has sat at 55.2% without moving since the start of the record, and the system has held 2 channels at 99% ever since. The daily laboratory check reads 66.7%. At the real clarity the water gets about 55 mJ/cm² against a target of 30: over twice the dose, paid for in lamp power.

lamps dimmed to the dose, minimum 50%, one channel below 7,600 m³/h

What it means

The clarity reading appears stuck, and the instrument appears to flag its own fault. The lamps are running hard because of it. Fix or recalibrate the analyser first, since dimming the lamps on a bad reading would be unsafe. Left alone, the lamps keep running at full power day and night.

What the operator does

Clean or replace the transmittance analyzer and verify it against the laboratory reading, then return the system to dose-paced control so lamps dim, and a channel drops out, at low flow.

How it is confirmed

UV kW per cubic metre treated and delivered dose. Target: dose near 30 mJ/cm², about 262 kW on average.

CAUSE 5

The blowers hold the air header higher than any basin needs

$77,118/yrmeasured

The air header is held at a fixed 67.5 kPa. The basins downstream of their valves need 61.6 kPa at most, so every basin valve throttles the difference away: the most-open valve sits at 68%. Each kilopascal the blowers do not have to make is power they do not draw. Letting the header follow the most-open valve, which is how most plants now run, takes 4.2 kPa off without changing any basin's air.

What the data shows

Header pressure
67.5 kPa
fixed setpoint
Highest basin need
61.6 kPa
pressure downstream of the basin valve, highest basin, sample by sample
Pressure throttled away
4.2 kPa
above the 1.7 kPa a control valve needs
Most-open basin valve
68 %
daily median; 85 to 90% is the usual target
Blower power saved
84 kW
4.9% of 1,724 kW, same air

What it means

The blowers make more pressure than any basin uses, and the valves waste the difference as heat. This is a control change, not new equipment, and no basin gets less air. Left alone, the blowers keep drawing that extra power every hour they run.

What the operator does

Replace the fixed header setpoint with most-open-valve control: lower the header pressure until the most open basin valve sits near 85 to 90%, and let it follow the load from there.

How it is confirmed

Header pressure, most-open valve position and blower kW per Nm³. Target: header near 63.3 kPa with the most-open valve at 85 to 90%.

CAUSE 6

Aeration basin 3 is held at more dissolved oxygen than the biology needs

$69,712/yrmeasured

Aeration basin 3 runs at 3.0 mg/L of dissolved oxygen; the 3 basins beside it, on the same feed and the same air header, run at 1.8. Its setpoint went from 1.8 to 3.0 on 18 June and has not come back. Oxygen dissolves more slowly the closer the water is to saturation, so the last part of that margin is the most expensive: the basin takes 18% more air than it would at its peers' level for the same treatment.

Nothing in the sewage reaching this basin asks for the higher oxygen level. The change came from a setting, and it has stayed since it was made. Left alone, the basin keeps paying for air it does not need. Check ammonia as you step the setting back, because the data cannot confirm that the lower level still removes it in every season.

CAUSE 7

Influent pump 3 is wearing out compared with its twins

$41,396/yrmeasured

Influent pump 3 does the same job as the pumps beside it. Measured at the terminals it now turns 13% less of its electrical power into flow and head than they do, after starting level with them. Vibration, drive end is up 89% against its twins, bearing temperature is up 15% against its twins, motor current is up 15% against its twins. Together that is wear, not the duty: impeller, wear rings or bearings, and it gets more expensive the longer it runs.

Plan influent pump 3's overhaul while its twins carry the duty: vibration spectrum this week, then impeller, wear rings and bearings at the next window.

One finding is not counted

They are shown because they are worth acting on this week. A meter error is money only once you know which meter is wrong; a safety finding has no price, and should not need one.

LEAD

The two influent flow meters have separated by 5.1%

$0measurednot counted in the total

The two meters on the influent flow agreed at the start of the record and now differ by 5.1%. It is a steady slide, not a process change, because a real change in flow would move both. 2 independent meters on the same water agree with meter B to within 0.4%; meter A reads 5.5% high. Influent flow is what the plant reports to its regulator and what member agencies are billed on.

What the data shows

Meter A against meter B
1.000 → 1.051
ratio, start to end
Meter B against the reference
+0.4 %
flow, flow
Meter A against the reference
+5.5 %
the one that is wrong

What it means

A steady slide between two meters points to one of them drifting, not to a change in the water. The independent check says meter A is the one reading high. Until it is corrected, reported flow and anything billed from it will be overstated.

What the operator does

Verify meter A against a portable reference before it is used again for permit reporting and billing member agencies.

How it is confirmed

The two meters and the reference. Target: within 1% of each other.

Where the plant is blind, a few probes close the gap

See the detail

Everything above came from instruments the plant already owns. A few things it cannot see at all: the load arriving at the basins between composites, whether the clarity reading behind the UV is still alive, and what an industrial discharger sends down the sewer. That is where AquaSpectra goes. It sits in the pipe and reads the water's full spectral fingerprint continuously. Its BOD reading is calibrated to the plant's own laboratory; everything else is change it learns against the plant's own results.

Is it right?

The audit was checked against the plant's own truth

See the detail

This plant is a physical simulation, built so the answer is known. Seven faults were built into it. The audit read only the historian export, the way it would read yours, and priced what it found. The simulator was then re-run with each fault removed, on the same weather and the same load, and the difference priced at the same unit costs. The audit never saw that.

The same plant with every fault removed audits at $0 of direct savings. Where the audit sits below the truth it is because it counts conservatively (a median night, a stated minimum valve pressure); where above, it is the twin it was compared with running slightly better than the fault-free plant would.

Quantities are read from 252 measuring points over 150 days. The record covers one season, so a full year of records would tighten every figure. Savings are ceilings that assume each fix is made and kept, and are not netted against the cost of making them, which is mostly labour the site already plans for.
